recipes.title: Rubrics that grade quickly and fairly
recipes.ai: Drafts a rubric from the spec and outcomes; you edit it
recipes.idea: Clear criteria make grading reliable and show students what good work looks like
recipes.ideaHtml: Clear criteria make grading reliable and show students what good work looks like (Jonsson and Svingby 2007)

recipes.title: Faster feedback with AI drafts and a person in the loop
recipes.ai: Drafts feedback against the rubric; a person reviews every one; students check it too, and earn credit for evidence that it is wrong
recipes.idea: Good feedback answers where am I going, how am I doing, where to next
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Good feedback answers where am I going, how am I doing, where to next (Hattie and Timperley 2007)

recipes.title: Low-stakes quizzes that teach
recipes.ai: Drafts questions from your materials, mixing in earlier topics; you check them
recipes.idea: Recalling something strengthens it more than rereading, and spreading practice over weeks makes it last
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Recalling something strengthens it more than rereading (Yang et al. 2021), and spreading practice over weeks makes it last (Cepeda et al. 2006)

recipes.title: Multiple-choice questions that find misconceptions
recipes.ai: Proposes wrong answers from common student errors
recipes.idea: Good items follow tested writing rules, and each wrong answer should mean something
recipes.ideaHtml: Good items follow tested writing rules, and each wrong answer should mean something (Haladyna et al. 2002)

recipes.title: Assignment specs students can follow
recipes.ai: Reads the spec as a student would and lists what is unclear
recipes.idea: Spelling out purpose, task and criteria helps underserved students most
recipes.ideaHtml: Spelling out purpose, task and criteria helps underserved students most (Winkelmes et al. 2016)

recipes.title: Worked examples, then practice
recipes.ai: Makes variants of a worked example with steps faded out
recipes.idea: Studying worked examples beats solving cold for novices
recipes.ideaHtml: Studying worked examples beats solving cold for novices (Atkinson et al. 2000)

recipes.title: An FAQ instead of a forum, fed by pre-class checks
recipes.ai: Groups the questions students write in reading checks and exit tickets into an FAQ you check and post before class; drafts announcements you approve
recipes.idea: Questions asked inside a reading check or exit ticket shape the next class, as in Just-in-Time Teaching, and reach the students who avoid asking in public
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Questions asked inside a reading check or exit ticket shape the next class, as in Just-in-Time Teaching (Novak 2011), and reach the students who avoid asking in public (Ryan et al. 2001)

recipes.title: Assignments and exams that measure the outcomes
recipes.ai: Maps each question and assignment to an outcome, and flags outcomes with fewer than two kinds of evidence
recipes.idea: Outcomes, teaching and assessment should line up, which is constructive alignment
recipes.ideaHtml: Outcomes, teaching and assessment should line up, which is constructive alignment (Biggs 1996)

recipes.title: Consistent grading across TAs
recipes.ai: Flags grades that do not match the rubric for a second look
recipes.idea: A grade is fair only if it measures the work, not who graded it
recipes.ideaHtml: A grade is fair only if it measures the work, not who graded it (Messick 1995)

recipes.title: Regrade requests without the pain
recipes.ai: Sorts requests against the rubric and drafts replies
recipes.idea: Feedback works as a dialogue, not a one-way message
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Feedback works as a dialogue, not a one-way message (Nicol 2010)

recipes.title: Formative assessment: acting on results while there is time
recipes.ai: Summarizes the common wrong answers across a class
recipes.idea: Assessment is formative when teacher and students act on what it shows, and it is among the strongest levers on learning
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Assessment is formative when teacher and students act on what it shows, and it is among the strongest levers on learning (Black and Wiliam 1998)

recipes.title: Peer review that helps both sides
recipes.ai: Drafts a review guide from the rubric
recipes.idea: Writing reviews teaches the reviewer as much as reading them
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Writing reviews teaches the reviewer as much as reading them (Nicol et al. 2014)

recipes.title: Grading final projects at scale
recipes.ai: Drafts a summary per team from the rubric and the repo history
recipes.idea: Students learn the standard by seeing it applied to their own work
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Students learn the standard by seeing it applied to their own work (Sadler 1989)

recipes.title: Reading your course evaluations
recipes.ai: Groups the open comments into themes
recipes.idea: Ratings track satisfaction more than learning, so read the comments for what to change
recipes.ideaHtml: Ratings track satisfaction more than learning, so read the comments for what to change (Uttl et al. 2017)

recipes.title: Course outcomes, each measured two ways
recipes.ai: Drafts outcomes with verbs you can assess, and suggests two kinds of evidence for each
recipes.idea: Bloom's revised taxonomy: name what students will be able to do
recipes.ideaHtml: Bloom's revised taxonomy: name what students will be able to do (Krathwohl 2002)

recipes.title: A syllabus and AI rules students read
recipes.ai: None needed: templates for AI levels and a disclosure statement
recipes.idea: Transparency again. Students do better when the rules and the purpose are explicit
recipes.ideaHtml: Transparency again. Students do better when the rules and the purpose are explicit (Winkelmes et al. 2016)

recipes.title: The first week: belonging
recipes.ai: Drafts a welcome survey and summarizes the answers
recipes.idea: A short message that struggle is normal raised grades for underrepresented students
recipes.ideaHtml: A short message that struggle is normal raised grades for underrepresented students (Walton and Cohen 2011)

recipes.title: Active learning in a large lecture
recipes.ai: Drafts in-class activities from your slides
recipes.idea: Active learning raises exam scores and cuts failure rates
recipes.ideaHtml: Active learning raises exam scores and cuts failure rates (Freeman et al. 2014)

recipes.title: Peer instruction
recipes.ai: Drafts concept questions from known misconceptions
recipes.idea: Vote, discuss, vote again, and students and teacher both see what is understood
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Vote, discuss, vote again, and students and teacher both see what is understood (Crouch and Mazur 2001)

recipes.title: Checking understanding by explaining back
recipes.ai: Short oral checks need none; AI interview tools are an option
recipes.idea: Explaining your own reasoning deepens it, the self-explanation effect
recipes.ideaHtml: Explaining your own reasoning deepens it, the self-explanation effect (Chi et al. 1989)

recipes.title: Parsons problems and live coding
recipes.ai: Turns solution code into Parsons problems
recipes.idea: Arranging given lines teaches as well as writing code, in less time
recipes.ideaHtml: Arranging given lines teaches as well as writing code, in less time (Ericson et al. 2017)

recipes.title: GitHub history that shows each student's own work
recipes.ai: Summarizes each student's commits, issues and pull requests for a quick check
recipes.idea: With AI everywhere, a grade has to be valid evidence of the student's own learning. Repository history shows how a student worked, such as testing as they go or working in small steps and starting early
recipes.ideaHtml: With AI everywhere, a grade has to be valid evidence of the student's own learning (Dawson et al. 2024). Repository history shows how a student worked, such as testing as they go (Kazerouni et al. 2019) or working in small steps and starting early (Kazerouni et al. 2017)

recipes.title: Running a course and its staff with Canvas and GitHub
recipes.ai: Drafts staff issues, checklists and Canvas pages from course data; you check them
recipes.idea: Much of running a large course is hidden logistics, and planning it ahead and writing it down is what prevents chaos
recipes.ideaHtml: Much of running a large course is hidden logistics, and planning it ahead and writing it down is what prevents chaos (Lim and Guo 2026)

recipes.title: Team projects that are fair to each student
recipes.ai: Summarizes contribution from GitHub and drafts team agreements
recipes.idea: Groups work when members depend on each other and each is accountable. Includes a protection clause, so a student who did their own part, with evidence, and reported the problem before the deadline is not marked down for a teammate's missing work
recipes.ideaHtml: Groups work when members depend on each other and each is accountable (Johnson and Johnson 2009). Includes a protection clause, so a student who did their own part, with evidence, and reported the problem before the deadline is not marked down for a teammate's missing work

recipes.title: Reaching students who fall behind
recipes.ai: Drafts check-in messages from Canvas activity; you send them
recipes.idea: "Wise" feedback pairs high standards with belief that the student can meet them
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. "Wise" feedback pairs high standards with belief that the student can meet them (Yeager et al. 2014)

recipes.title: TAs, feedback and AI
recipes.ai: Guidance and a template for TA expectations
recipes.idea: Feedback works only when students can take it up, and TAs give most of it
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Feedback works only when students can take it up, and TAs give most of it (Carless and Boud 2018)

recipes.title: Students giving themselves feedback
recipes.ai: Drafts reflection prompts and exam wrappers; students also check AI feedback on their own work
recipes.idea: Self-regulated learners plan, check and adjust their own work, and judging AI output is part of that now
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Self-regulated learners plan, check and adjust their own work (Zimmerman 2002), and judging AI output is part of that now (Bearman et al. 2024)

recipes.title: Revising your course from the evidence
recipes.ai: Pulls grades, comments and feedback into one page, outcome by outcome
recipes.idea: Close the loop by lining outcomes, teaching and assessment up again
recipes.ideaHtml: Close the loop by lining outcomes, teaching and assessment up again (Biggs 1996)

recipes.title: Onboarding course staff in one week
recipes.ai: Drafts a staff handbook from your syllabus and last term's notes
recipes.idea: Computing TAs across Europe describe the challenges of the job, many of them about working with the course rather than with students
recipes.ideaHtml: Computing TAs across Europe describe the challenges of the job, many of them about working with the course rather than with students (Riese et al. 2021)

recipes.title: A 30-minute weekly staff meeting
recipes.ai: Drafts the agenda from the week's issues, deadlines and forum
recipes.idea: Planning the logistics ahead, in writing, is what keeps a large course calm
recipes.ideaHtml: Planning the logistics ahead, in writing, is what keeps a large course calm (Lim and Guo 2026)

recipes.title: Give each TA a role, not a pile
recipes.ai: None needed: a role template (grading lead, forum lead, lab lead, student check-ins)
recipes.idea: Teams work when each member is accountable for a part, and that holds for course staff too
recipes.ideaHtml: Teams work when each member is accountable for a part (Johnson and Johnson 2009), and that holds for course staff too

recipes.title: When AI drafts the grading, what TAs do instead
recipes.ai: AI drafts the feedback (Recipe 2); TAs review it and move the hours saved to students
recipes.idea: Review has to be real, because TAs who over-relied on AI drafts passed on its errors; feedback only works when students take it up
recipes.ideaHtml: Review has to be real, because TAs who over-relied on AI drafts passed on its errors (Ahmed et al. 2025); feedback only works when students take it up (Carless and Boud 2018)

recipes.title: Turning grading hours into student contact
recipes.ai: Estimates the hours saved per assignment and drafts a staff schedule that spends them on students
recipes.idea: Contact with faculty outside class is linked to students' learning gains
recipes.ideaHtml: Contact with faculty outside class is linked to students' learning gains (Kuh and Hu 2001)

recipes.title: Alternatives to office hours
recipes.ai: Shows when students submit and ask questions, so help goes where and when it is needed
recipes.idea: Office hours redesigned around students' needs got more use; students stay away when they do not see what a visit is for
recipes.ideaHtml: Office hours redesigned around students' needs got more use (Wetzel 2025); students stay away when they do not see what a visit is for (Griffin et al. 2014)

recipes.title: Reasons to come to office hours
recipes.ai: None needed for the incentives: a first-visit credit, points back for evidence against AI feedback (Recipe 2), and a small end-of-term boost based on the interaction log (Recipe 39)
recipes.idea: Students who came to office hours did better in the course
recipes.ideaHtml: Students who came to office hours did better in the course (Guerrero and Rod 2013)

recipes.title: Office hours that teach, not just fix bugs
recipes.ai: Drafts a hint ladder for each assignment, so staff guide rather than fix
recipes.idea: Knowing what students actually bring to office hours shows what help TAs give and could give
recipes.ideaHtml: Knowing what students actually bring to office hours shows what help TAs give and could give (Ren et al. 2019)

recipes.title: Undergraduate course assistants: training and support
recipes.ai: Drafts practice scenarios for role-play in staff training
recipes.idea: Tutoring depends on reading the student's thinking, which can be practiced
recipes.ideaHtml: Tutoring depends on reading the student's thinking, which can be practiced (Markel and Guo 2021)

recipes.title: One answer from every staff member
recipes.ai: Keeps a staff FAQ up to date from the forum and the pre-class checks (Recipe 7)
recipes.idea: A shared written record is what lets every TA give the same, timely answer
recipes.ideaHtml: A shared written record is what lets every TA give the same, timely answer (Lim and Guo 2026)

recipes.title: A log of every student interaction, for fair decisions
recipes.ai: Logs each office-hours visit, message, extension and meeting in one record per student, and summarizes a student's term when a decision or a final grade adjustment comes up; you decide
recipes.idea: Fair decisions need consistent procedures and explanations students can follow, not only fair outcomes. A complete record makes extensions, appeals and end-of-term boosts consistent across students and across the term, and makes coming to office hours count
recipes.ideaHtml: Fair decisions need consistent procedures and explanations students can follow, not only fair outcomes (Rasooli et al. 2019). A complete record makes extensions, appeals and end-of-term boosts consistent across students and across the term, and makes coming to office hours count

recipes.title: Midsemester feedback from students and staff
recipes.ai: Groups the open comments into themes and drafts your reply to the class
recipes.idea: Acting on midterm student feedback improved end-of-term teaching ratings
recipes.ideaHtml: Acting on midterm student feedback improved end-of-term teaching ratings (Cohen 1980)

recipes.title: Keeping staff hours in check
recipes.ai: Totals staff hours from the staff issues against the contract
recipes.idea: Overlapping threads of work were the main source of TA stress
recipes.ideaHtml: Overlapping threads of work were the main source of TA stress (Lim and Guo 2026)

recipes.title: Handing the course to next term
recipes.ai: Drafts a course playbook from the term's issues, announcements and notes
recipes.idea: Close the loop at the level of the course as well as the class
recipes.ideaHtml: Close the loop at the level of the course as well as the class (Biggs 1996)

recipes.title: Exams students can prepare for
recipes.ai: Checks your questions against the blueprint and drafts practice questions that combine topics; you write the real exam
recipes.idea: Recalling from memory beats rereading, even with no feedback, and a concept map drawn from memory works like a practice test
recipes.ideaHtml: Feedback. Recalling from memory beats rereading, even with no feedback (Roediger and Karpicke 2006), and a concept map drawn from memory works like a practice test (Blunt and Karpicke 2014)

recipes.title: A syllabus that runs the semester for you
recipes.ai: Checks a draft against the Senate's 14 required elements and drafts the calendar backward from fixed dates
recipes.idea: Rules and purpose spelled out help most the students who need them, and the university requires them
recipes.ideaHtml: Rules and purpose spelled out help most the students who need them (Winkelmes et al. 2016), and the university requires them (UMass Amherst Faculty Senate 2024)

problems.grading-consistency: Grades differ from one grader to another
problems.slow-feedback: Feedback reaches students too late to use
problems.forum: The forum or inbox eats staff time
problems.office-hours: Few students come to office hours
problems.ai-worry: I worry students hand their work to AI
problems.exams: My exams do not match what I teach, or carry too much weight
problems.teams: Team projects are unfair or chaotic
problems.falling-behind: Students fall behind before I notice
problems.staff: Coordinating TAs takes too much of my time
problems.design: I am designing or redesigning a course
problems.fairness: I want decisions about students to be consistent and fair

goals.feedback: More and faster feedback for students
goals.formative: Find out what students understand while there is time to act
